title: Facing the Press

narrative.text: The press room is a converted ministerial office with twenty-three chairs arranged in three rows, microphones from four radio stations, and a lectern that is slightly too tall for you. The room is full. Every seat is occupied and journalists are standing along the walls and in the doorway. The camera crews have set up in the back with the particular stillness of people who have been told not to move until the Chancellor speaks. Nadia Voss is in the front row, second seat from the left. She has a notebook open and a pen in her hand and the expression of someone who has been waiting for exactly this moment.

You step to the lectern. The room quiets — not completely, but enough. The camera red lights come on. Vyktor is standing against the back wall, arms crossed, watching the room the way a general watches a battlefield. He told you before you walked in: three questions, five minutes, no follow-ups. You know he is wrong about the follow-ups. The press does not accept no-follow-ups. The press accepts whatever it decides to accept.

Chancellor. The referendum passed — fifty-one to fifty-nine percent depending on which province you count. Was this a mandate, or was it a warning? Half the country voted against the constitution you staked your government on. Kolvar has called it 'a narrow endorsement of a flawed document.' The Iron Covenant has issued no statement, which in itself is a statement. What does this result actually mean for your ability to govern?

She opens with the hardest question. Of course she does. Nadia Voss does not ease into interviews — she begins where other journalists end. The referendum margin is the number everyone is thinking about and no one wants to say aloud: it is thin enough to be contested and large enough to be claimed. She is asking me to choose which one it is, in front of every camera in the capital. The answer I give will be the headline by dinner.

monologue: Nadia opens with the hardest question. The referendum margin — thin enough to contest, large enough to claim. She's asking me to choose which one it is, in front of every camera in the capital. The answer I give becomes the headline by dinner.

choices.text: "The margin is what democracy looks like when it works. Sixty percent voted for reform. Forty percent wanted something different. Both numbers are real. Both are Veltrians. The constitution passed because more people wanted it than didn't — and I will govern for all of them, including the ones who voted no. That is not a warning, Ms. Voss. That is a republic functioning as designed."

reactions.text: She writes something in her notebook without looking up. The pen moves fast — she is not transcribing, she is composing. When she looks up, there is something in her expression that might be respect or might be the particular alertness of a journalist who has just been given a quote worth building a story around.

choices.text: "The margin is narrow. I know that. Forty-eight percent of Veltrians looked at the constitution I spent twenty-six weeks negotiating and said no. I hear them. The constitution is the law now — the vote was clear on that — but governing does not end at fifty percent. I will spend the next year demonstrating that this document works for the people who doubted it, not just the people who supported it."

reactions.text: She nods — once, small, the nod of someone who has heard a measured answer and is filing it for later comparison against future actions. Her pen stops. She does not write anything down. The silence is her way of saying: I will remember this, and I will hold you to it.

choices.text: "What the referendum means is that Veltria now has a constitutional framework for the first time in its history. The question is not what the margin means — the question is what we do with the document the people approved. I am focused on implementation, not on parsing the political significance of a vote that has already been counted."

reactions.text: Chancellor, with respect — you did not answer the question. The margin is the story. Every newspaper in this city will lead with the margin. The question is whether your government treats forty-eight percent opposition as a mandate or as a problem. Which is it?

choices.text: "Ms. Voss, the margin is fifty-one percent. In a democracy, that is a majority. I notice you did not ask Kolvar what his margin was when the Halvekists won elections with sixty percent of eligible voters staying home. The referendum was free, it was fair, and it was decisive. If you are looking for a story about division, I suggest you look at the forty-eight percent who voted against — and ask them why they are not the ones you are questioning."

reactions.text: She does not blink. She does not look away. She holds your gaze for exactly three seconds — long enough for the cameras to capture the exchange, long enough for the room to register that something has happened — and then she writes a single line in her notebook. She does not ask a follow-up. She does not need to. The silence is her way of telling you that she has just decided what the story is about.
